body:
Development must improve life without destroying its foundations

Development is a process through which people gain better living conditions, opportunities and capabilities. Higher income, increased production, better health, education, employment, housing and access to essential services can all contribute to development. However, economic growth alone does not establish that development is sustainable.

Suppose an agricultural region increases its production by extracting large quantities of groundwater. Farmers may earn more income in the short term. If groundwater extraction continuously exceeds natural recharge, however, wells may become deeper or dry up, irrigation costs may rise and future farmers may find it difficult to cultivate their land. The immediate economic gain has been achieved partly by reducing the resources available for future use.

This example shows why development must be judged by both its present benefits and its long-term consequences.

The Brundtland definition

The World Commission on Environment and Development, chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland, published its report Our Common Future in 1987. The report established the widely accepted definition of sustainable development:

Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

The definition contains 2 particularly important ideas. First, present development must address human needs, especially the essential needs of people living in poverty. Second, meeting present needs must not destroy the environmental conditions and resources on which future generations will depend.

The report also recognizes that technology and social organization affect the environment's ability to meet present and future needs. Sustainable development therefore requires changes in production, consumption, technology and institutions, not simply the protection of unused natural resources.

Why the environment is essential to the economy

Human economic activity depends upon the environment in several ways:

  • Resource supply: Forests provide timber, agricultural land produces food, rivers supply water and mineral deposits provide raw materials.
  • Waste assimilation: Natural processes can absorb or break down some wastes, but this capacity is limited. Pollution becomes a serious problem when waste generation exceeds the environment's ability to assimilate it safely.
  • Life-support functions: Ecosystems help maintain climate conditions, nutrient cycling, soil formation and biological diversity.
  • Aesthetic and cultural services: Landscapes, forests, rivers and other natural environments provide recreational and cultural benefits.

Because these functions support human well-being and economic production, environmental degradation can create economic losses. Polluted water increases treatment and health costs. Soil erosion reduces agricultural productivity. Loss of vegetation can increase flood and erosion risks.

Economic growth and sustainable development are different

Economic growth generally refers to an increase in the production of goods and services, commonly measured through real gross domestic product. Sustainable development is broader: it considers the quality and distribution of development benefits, the condition of the environment and the ability to maintain well-being over time.

Growth may help finance better health care, education, sanitation and environmental protection. Nevertheless, growth is not automatically inclusive or environmentally sustainable. A country can experience rising income alongside severe air pollution, resource depletion or unequal access to basic services.

Sustainable development does not mean that economic activity must stop. It means that economic and social progress should occur without undermining the ecological systems and resource base needed to sustain human well-being.

The central question

Every major development decision involves a combination of benefits, costs and responsibilities. A useful assessment asks whether the activity improves people's lives, whether its benefits and costs are distributed fairly, and whether the natural systems supporting those benefits can continue to function.

For example, expanding irrigation may improve food production and farmers' incomes. Its sustainability also depends on equitable access to water, the efficiency of irrigation, groundwater recharge and the prevention of soil salinity. A project that succeeds economically but causes serious long-term environmental damage cannot be judged solely by its initial output.

Prelims focus

  • The Brundtland Report was titled Our Common Future and was published in 1987.
  • It was prepared by the World Commission on Environment and Development.
  • The definition emphasizes present needs and the needs of future generations.
  • Environmental functions include resource supply, waste assimilation, life support and aesthetic services.
  • Trap: An increase in GDP does not, by itself, prove sustainable development.

[World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future (1987), Chapter 2, Section I, paragraphs 1–2; NCERT, Class 11, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 164–172; NCERT, Class 12, India: People and Economy, Chapter 9, Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context, printed pp. 108–110; United Nations, Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, Preamble and paragraphs 2–5, consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: The Meaning and Foundations of Sustainable Development

body:
Economic, social and environmental sustainability

Sustainable development requires attention to 3 interconnected dimensions: economic, social and environmental. These are not independent objectives that can be achieved without considering their effects on one another.

Economic dimension

Economic sustainability concerns the ability of an economy to support productive activities, employment, income and essential services over time. It includes the efficient use of resources, productive infrastructure and the avoidance of development patterns that create serious long-term costs.

For example, an industry that improves productivity while reducing energy and material waste may strengthen its economic position and reduce pressure on resources.

Social dimension

Social sustainability concerns human well-being, equality, dignity and access to opportunities. It includes reducing poverty, improving health and education, ensuring safe working conditions and addressing discrimination and exclusion.

Development is socially incomplete when its benefits reach only a small section of society while other groups remain without basic services.

Environmental dimension

Environmental sustainability concerns the conservation of resources and the continued functioning of ecological systems. It includes maintaining biodiversity, preventing pollution, protecting soil and water, and reducing activities that destabilize the climate.

A renewable resource must also be managed sustainably. A forest may regenerate naturally, but repeated extraction beyond its capacity to regenerate can still cause degradation.

Consider a village irrigation project. Its economic dimension includes crop production and farming income. Its social dimension includes whether small farmers and disadvantaged households receive fair access to water. Its environmental dimension includes protecting groundwater, soil and nearby ecosystems. A successful decision considers all 3 dimensions together.

Intergenerational and intragenerational equity

Equity means fairness in the distribution of opportunities, benefits, burdens and access to resources. Sustainable development applies this principle both across time and among people living today.

PrincipleWhose interests are considered?Example
Intergenerational equityPresent and future generationsProtecting groundwater and forests so that future people can meet their needs.
Intragenerational equityDifferent people and groups within the present generationEnsuring affordable drinking water for poor and remote households.

Intergenerational equity

Present generations inherit natural resources, ecosystems, infrastructure and knowledge from earlier generations. Their decisions affect what future generations will inherit. Intergenerational equity requires present societies to consider these future consequences.

For instance, excessive groundwater extraction may benefit current users while imposing additional costs on future users. Similarly, destruction of a natural habitat may remove ecological functions that are difficult or impossible to restore.

Intragenerational equity

People living at the same time do not have equal access to income, resources, public services or protection from environmental harm. Intragenerational equity focuses on reducing such inequalities.

For example, a water-supply scheme may increase the total amount of water delivered to a district but still leave remote settlements without reliable access. In that situation, average improvement does not establish equitable development.

How the 2 forms of equity are connected

Protecting resources for the future should not mean ignoring the basic needs of people living in poverty today. Equally, meeting urgent present needs should not justify avoidable environmental destruction that deprives future generations.

Sustainable policies therefore seek to provide essential services while preserving the ecological conditions required to continue providing them. Efficient irrigation, equitable water allocation, improved sanitation and protection of local water sources can contribute to both forms of equity.

The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development commits countries to leave no one behind and to endeavour to reach the furthest behind first. This principle links sustainable development with the identification of people who are excluded from progress.

Fairness in measuring development

A district-wide average can conceal important inequalities. If most households in a city have reliable drinking water but remote villages do not, the district average may give an incomplete picture. Data separated by location, income group, sex, age or other relevant characteristics can help identify which groups have not benefited.

Thus, equity is not merely an ethical addition to sustainable development. It affects how priorities are selected, how public services are delivered and how progress is measured.

Prelims focus

  • The 3 dimensions are economic, social and environmental.
  • Intergenerational equity concerns fairness between present and future generations.
  • Intragenerational equity concerns fairness among people living in the same generation.
  • The 2030 Agenda includes the commitment to leave no one behind.
  • Trap: Protecting future resources alone does not satisfy the requirement to address present poverty and inequality.

[NCERT, Class 12, India: People and Economy, Chapter 9, Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context, printed pp. 108–111; NCERT, Class 11, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 171–172; World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future (1987), Chapter 2, Section I; United Nations General Assembly, Resolution 70/1, Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (2015), Preamble and paragraphs 4–5, consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: The Three Dimensions of Sustainable Development and the Principle of Equity

body:
What is natural capital?

Natural capital refers to the stock of natural resources and ecosystems that provides benefits to people. It includes forests, soil, water, minerals, biodiversity and the ecological processes that support life and economic activity.

Other forms of capital also contribute to development. Produced capital includes machinery, roads and buildings. Human capital includes people's knowledge, health and skills. These forms of capital can work together to produce goods, services and well-being.

The distinction between weak and strong sustainability concerns whether the loss of natural capital can be compensated for by increasing other forms of capital.

Weak sustainability

Weak sustainability permits substitution between natural capital and produced or human capital, provided that the overall capacity to support human well-being is maintained.

Under this approach, using some natural resources may be considered compatible with sustainability if the benefits are invested in other productive assets that preserve the capacity of future generations to meet their needs.

For example, income obtained from extracting a non-renewable resource might be invested in education, infrastructure or technology. The weak-sustainability approach allows such substitution in principle.

However, the argument depends on whether the replacement assets can genuinely compensate for the lost benefits. It does not establish that every environmental loss can be offset simply by spending money elsewhere.

Strong sustainability

Strong sustainability recognizes that some forms of natural capital perform essential functions that cannot be adequately replaced by produced or human capital. Such natural capital must be maintained or protected within appropriate ecological limits.

A forest may supply timber, absorb carbon, support biodiversity, maintain soil and influence local water flows. A plantation or water-treatment facility may replace some of these services, but it does not necessarily reproduce the full range of functions performed by the original forest ecosystem.

Critical natural capital refers to those natural assets or processes whose essential functions are difficult or impossible to substitute adequately. Examples may include ecosystems supporting irreplaceable biodiversity or natural processes necessary for stable life-support conditions.

The central distinction

The 2 approaches differ mainly in the degree of substitutability they accept.

  • Weak sustainability: The combined stock of different forms of capital or their capacity to generate well-being is the main concern.
  • Strong sustainability: Maintaining critical natural capital and essential ecological functions is an additional requirement, even when other forms of capital increase.

Both approaches recognize that uncontrolled resource use can threaten long-term well-being. Their disagreement concerns how much natural capital may safely be replaced.

Applying the distinction

Suppose a wetland is proposed for conversion into an industrial area. The project may generate employment, roads and income. A weak-sustainability assessment may emphasize whether the increased economic and social benefits compensate for the environmental loss.

A strong-sustainability assessment would also ask whether the wetland performs critical functions such as supporting biodiversity, storing floodwater or maintaining local ecological conditions. If those functions cannot be adequately replaced, the conversion may be considered unsustainable even when the project generates substantial income.

The weak-versus-strong distinction is an analytical framework, not a rule that every resource has a fixed classification. Whether a particular natural function can be replaced depends on the resource, the available technology, ecological conditions and the consequences of its loss.

Connection with development policy

The debate helps explain why environmental assessment cannot rely exclusively on monetary costs and benefits. Certain losses may be difficult to value, irreversible or associated with ecological thresholds. Protecting such functions can be necessary even when compensation for some economic losses is possible.

At the same time, investments in education, public health, clean technology and infrastructure can help societies reduce their dependence on environmentally damaging activities. Sustainable policy therefore requires both the protection of essential ecological systems and improvements in human capabilities.

Prelims focus

  • Natural capital includes natural resources, ecosystems and their useful functions.
  • Weak sustainability allows substitution between different forms of capital.
  • Strong sustainability emphasizes protection of essential and non-substitutable natural capital.
  • Critical natural capital provides functions that cannot be adequately replaced.
  • Trap: Planting trees or constructing infrastructure does not necessarily replace every ecological function lost when a natural forest is destroyed.

[European Environment Agency, Exiting the Anthropocene? Exploring fundamental change in our relationship with nature, discussion of weak and strong sustainability, consulted 1 November 2026; European Commission, Communication COM(2000) 576, discussion of natural, human and physical capital and alternative definitions of sustainability, consulted 1 November 2026; NCERT, Class 11, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 171–172.]
